name: Hook-and-line and open-sea fishing in Timor and Alor
summary: People at Jerimalai in Timor-Leste caught open-sea fish about 42,000 years ago, and a shell fishhook there lay in deposits 23,000 to 16,000 years old.
description: Fish remains from Jerimalai shelter (now also called Asitau Kuru) at the eastern tip of Timor include pelagic species such as tuna and date to 42,000 years before the present; the excavators argue that catching them needed planning and complex maritime technology, though how the earliest fish were caught is not established. A single-piece shell fishhook from the same shelter comes from a deposit dated between about 23,000 and 16,000 calibrated years ago, and five shell hooks buried with a woman at Tron Bon Lei on Alor Island include one directly dated to about 11,300–11,100 calibrated years ago. A hook of 23,000–20,000 calibrated years ago from Okinawa is described by the same excavators as the oldest known.

impact.note: Hook-and-line and offshore fishing was a new capability for island communities in Wallacea; reach stays regional and generativity is 0 because no source read shows later fishing elsewhere descending from it.

date.label: c. 42,000 years ago (c. 40,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Remains of pelagic and other fish from Jerimalai shelter in East Timor date to 42,000 years before the present (about 40,050 BCE).

evidence.supports: remains of a variety of pelagic and other fish species dating to 42,000 years before the present from Jerimalai shelter in East Timor

date.label: c. 23,000–16,000 cal BP (c. 21,050–14,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: A shell fishhook from Jerimalai shelter in Timor-Leste comes from a deposit dated between about 23,000 and 16,000 calibrated years before present (about 21,050–14,050 BCE).

evidence.supports: Another shell hook from Jerimalai Shelter in Timor-Leste is of a comparable age to the Okinawa find, in a deposit context dated to between c. 23000 and 16000 cal BP

date.label: 11,310–11,075 cal BP (c. 9360–9125 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: One of the shell fishhooks buried with a woman at the Tron Bon Lei rockshelter on Alor Island was directly radiocarbon dated to 11,310–11,075 calibrated years before present (about 9360–9125 BCE).

evidence.supports: An AMS radiocarbon date of 11310–11075 cal BP (S-ANU-41825: 10230±30 BP) on hook C is consistent with a date on a fragment of charcoal from within the left eye socket of the individual of 12035–11500 cal BP
evidence.locator: Section 'AMS dating of the Tron Bon Lei burial context and grave goods'; the article's title and abstract place the burial at Tron Bon Lei on Alor Island

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The 2011 Science paper was read only as an abstract; the Jerimalai hook's context and dates are taken from the excavators' 2017 summary of it and should be checked in the original.
Whether the fish caught 42,000 years ago were taken with hooks, nets or lures is not settled by the abstract.
The 2017 paper also gives a hook from Lene Hara Cave, Timor-Leste, directly dated to about 11,000 calibrated years ago; it has no event here.
The Jerimalai coordinates are approximate and need checking against a gazetteer; the Tron Bon Lei shelter is placed only at island level because the paper read gives no coordinates.

research.note: The 2011 study called its hooks the earliest definite evidence of fishhook manufacture, but the excavators' own 2017 paper and Fujita et al. 2016 give the oldest example as a hook from Sakitari Cave, Okinawa (about 23,000-20,000 calibrated years ago); no link between the two is shown, and the 2017 paper reads similar hooks elsewhere as convergence.
